Question nine. What is a context window, and why does its size matter? It's the most tokens, prompt and output together, that the model can attend to at once. Instructions, documents and history all compete for it, a longer one costs more, and anything past the limit is invisible. So much for the shape. Next, how it learns.

Question ten. What is pretraining, and what objectives are used? Training on a huge unlabeled corpus, where the text is its own label. Masked language modeling, bert's, hides tokens and predicts them from both sides. Causal language modeling, GPT's, predicts the next token from the left alone, which is what lets it generate.

Question eleven. What is the difference between pretraining and fine-tuning? Pretraining is the expensive phase, once per model. Fine-tuning cheaply adapts it to one task, on a much smaller labeled set. Instruction tuning and RLHF, reinforcement learning from human feedback, then teach it to follow instructions and match human preferences. Even fine-tuning can be made far cheaper.

Question twelve. What is parameter-efficient fine-tuning, for example laura? Laura, low-rank adaptation, freezes the model and learns an update to some of its matrices, as the product of two thin ones. A matrix four thousand and ninety-six square holds nearly seventeen million numbers. At rank eight, the two thin ones hold sixty-five thousand: under half a percent. Adapt two matrices in each of thirty-two layers, and you train about four million weights out of six and a half billion, and ship an eight-megabyte adapter instead of a thirteen-gigabyte copy. At serving, merge it into the weights and it adds no latency, or keep it separate, and one base model serves many adapters. Fine-tuning changes how a model behaves. What it knows is another matter.
